Chapter Seven. The Tyranny of Authority and the Quiet Acts of Defiance.
As the boy grew older, school didn’t just get more complicated—it started to feel like a world ruled by its own set of laws. Suddenly, teachers weren’t just distant adults anymore. Their authority felt bigger, heavier. Sure, some used that power to guide and encourage, to help their students grow. But there were others, and you could spot them a mile away—the ones who seemed to enjoy the control, who turned discipline into something sharp and cold. The line between keeping order and crossing into cruelty? Well, it was thin. And more than once, the boy found himself on the wrong side of it.
There was a headmaster everyone feared. Just his presence could change the mood in a hallway. His punishments? People whispered about them. His temper? Completely unpredictable. So, the students learned to keep their heads down, to move quietly, to read the room before they spoke or even breathed too loudly. But here’s the thing—under all that careful silence, resistance simmered.
Passing notes in class, whispering jokes, even finding clever ways to bend the rules—these little rebellions weren’t just for laughs. They were tiny ways to take back power, to remind themselves they still had choices.
One day, something happened that stuck with the boy. A classmate was singled out—punished for something that just felt wrong. It was harsh, and everyone else looked away, too scared to step in. But the boy felt something shift inside him. He realized that sometimes, staying silent is its own kind of agreement with what’s happening. So, later that night, back in the dormitory where it felt safer, he offered a quiet word of comfort, a small gesture to show that his friend wasn’t alone.
It may not have seemed like much, but in that moment, it truly mattered. Courage, he learned, isn’t always about grand gestures. Sometimes, it’s found in the quiet support you offer when someone needs it most.
The adults, of course, seemed oblivious to all this. They handed out punishments, enforced the rules, and assumed everything was under control. But the students knew better. Real authority doesn’t come from making people afraid. It comes from respect. The teachers who inspired loyalty? They were the ones who listened, who treated each student as an individual, who could see the potential hiding in every child.
Looking back, those years weren’t just about surviving heavy-handed authority. They were about learning how to navigate power, how to spot injustice, and—most importantly—how to push back, even if it was just in small, subtle ways.
The lessons the boy learned during those times? They’d echo through his whole life, shaping how he faced challenges, and how he treated the people around him.
